TABRISI:6:76-79#2/r9.anchor: واختلف في الكوكب الذي رآه فقيل هو الزهرة. وقيل: هو المشتري

TABRISI:6:76-79#3/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:76-79#3/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:76-79#3/r6.claim: The first view need not make Abraham falsely claim knowledge: he may have posed the claim hypothetically, as one supposes a body's eternity to expose the absurdity of that assumption.
TABRISI:6:76-79#3/r6.anchor: أنه لم يقل ذلك مخبرا وإنما قاله فارضا ومقدرا على سبيل التأمل

TABRISI:6:76-79#3/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:76-79#3/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:76-79#3/r7.claim: Alternatively, he reported a thought he could provisionally entertain during inquiry and then abandon when evidence refuted it.
TABRISI:6:76-79#3/r7.anchor: أخبر عن ظنة قد يجوز أن يظن المتفكر في حال فكره ونظره ما لا أصل له

TABRISI:6:76-79#3/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:76-79#3/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:76-79#3/r8.claim: A report says Abraham's mother gave birth in a cave to hide him from Nimrod, so he may not have seen the sky before leaving it; alternatively, he may have seen it without yet reflecting on its signs because reflection was not yet obligatory.
TABRISI:6:76-79#3/r8.anchor: قد روي أنه أمه كانت ولدته في مغارة خوفا من أن يقتله نمرود

TABRISI:6:76-78/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:76-78/r3.speaker: أوس بن حجر
TABRISI:6:76-78/r3.claim: Aws ibn Ḥajar's line is cited as an example of dropping the interrogative hamza.
TABRISI:6:76-78/r3.anchor:
قال أوس بن حجر:
لعمرك لا أدري وإن كنت داريا شعيب بن شهم أم شعيب بن منقر

TABRISI:6:76-78/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:76-78/r4.speaker: الأخطل
TABRISI:6:76-78/r4.claim: Al-Akhṭal's line is another example of an omitted interrogative hamza.
TABRISI:6:76-78/r4.anchor:
وقال الأخطل:
كذبتك عينك أم رأيت بواسط غلس الظلام من الرباب خيالا

TABRISI:6:76-78/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:76-78/r5.speaker: عمر بن أبي ربيعة
TABRISI:6:76-78/r5.claim: ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa's line means did you love her, illustrating the omitted hamza.
TABRISI:6:76-78/r5.anchor:
وقال عمر بن أبي ربيعة:
ثم قالوا تحبها قلت بهرا

TABRISI:6:76-78/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:76-78/r6.speaker: شاعر
TABRISI:6:76-78/r6.claim: An unnamed poet's line similarly means are they them, with the question hamza omitted.
TABRISI:6:76-78/r6.anchor:
وقال آخر:
رفوني وقالوا يا خويلد لا ترع فقلت وأنكرت الوجوه هم هم

TABRISI:6:76-78/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:76-78/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:6:76-78/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the phrase in 90:11 as a question meaning did he not scale the obstacle, with the hamza omitted.
TABRISI:6:76-78/r7.anchor: معناه أفلا اقتحم فحذف حرف الاستفهام

THALABI:v4p161/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p161/r12.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p161/r12.claim: The passage moves from God's making Abraham certain to the nightfall scene in which he sees a star and the account continues.
THALABI:v4p161/r12.anchor: وليكون من الموقنين فلما جن عليه الليل رأى كوكبا إلى آخر الآية.

THALABI:v4p161/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p161/r13.speaker: المفسرون
THALABI:v4p161/r13.claim: The commentators say Abraham was born under Nimrod ibn Canaan, who was first to wear a crown; astrologers predicted a boy would change earthly religion and end Nimrod's rule, a forecast they said was in prophetic books.
THALABI:v4p161/r13.anchor: قال المفسرون: إن إبراهيم (عليه السلام) ولد في زمن نمرود بن كنعان وكان نمرود أول من وضع التاج على رأسه

THALABI:v4p161/r14.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p161/r14.speaker: الكهان والمنجمون
THALABI:v4p161/r14.claim: Nimrod's astrologers warned that a boy born that year would change the world's religion and bring about Nimrod's death and loss of rule.
THALABI:v4p161/r14.anchor: وكان له كهان ومنجمون. وقالوا: إنه يولد في بلدك هذه السنة غلام يغير دين أهل الأرض

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r1.claim: The common reading opens both rāʾ and hamza; for readers who otherwise use imāla, loss of the following alif removes the cause for tilting the hamza and thus the rāʾ vowel.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r1.anchor: وهو قراءة العامة، ووجه ذلك أنه الأصل على قراءة من فتحهما إذا لم يلقه ساكن

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r2.claim: The rāʾ is opened here though read with kasra in ‘raʾā kawkaban’ because the reader uses both dialectal forms, treating this rāʾ like the one in ramā and raʿā.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r2.anchor: فتح الراء هاهنا وقد كسره في {رأى كوكبا} فلأنه أخذ باللغتين

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r3.speaker: حمزة وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r3.claim: Ḥamza and ʿĀṣim in Abū Bakr's transmission read with kasra on rāʾ and fatḥa on hamza; the rāʾ kasra follows the stated underlying analysis and is independent of hamza imāla.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r3.anchor: وهي قراءة حمزة وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر (¬3)، أما كسر الراء فإنما هو للتنزيل

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r4.speaker: يحيى بن آدم عن أبي بكر
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r4.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Ādam reports Abū Bakr reading both rāʾ and hamza with kasra; the deleted alif remains conceptually present because it was dropped to avoid two adjacent vowelless consonants, like the cited poetic construction.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r4.anchor: وروى يحيى بن (¬4) آدم عن أبي بكر (¬5): {رأى القمر}: بكسر الراء والهمزة معا

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r5.claim: The story related by al-Suddī, Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, and historians says Abraham left the cave where he was born, reflected on creatures and the heavens, and recognized their creator and provider as his Lord before seeing the star.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r5.anchor: فقال السدي (¬3)، ومحمد بن إسحاق (¬4) # والعلماء بأخبار الماضين: (8) (لما شب إبراهيم في السرب

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r6.speaker: السدي ومحمد بن إسحاق والعلماء بأخبار الماضين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r6.claim: In that account, the first celestial body Abraham saw was Jupiter, though another version calls it Venus; he saw it before the moon near the end of the month.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p242/r6.anchor: ثم نظر فإذا المشتري قد طلع، ويقال: الزهرة، وكانت تلك الليلة في آخر الشهر

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r1.speaker: أهل التحقيق من العلماء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r1.claim: The verifying scholars reject any account in which Abraham was ever confused or idolatrous: God protected him, he was already a prophet, and the ‘sound heart’ verse means he never associated partners; revelation of the kingdom makes subsequent belief in a star impossible.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r1.anchor: فقال أهل التحقيق من العلماء: (إن إبراهيم عليه السلام لم يكن قط في ضلال وحيرة

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r2.claim: On the principal explanation, Abraham said ‘this is my Lord’ to draw his star-worshipping people into the argument, then expose the error of revering stars and assigning them power over events.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r2.anchor: وإنما معنى قوله: {هذا ربي} أن قومه كانوا يعبدون النجوم ويعظمونها ويحكمون بها

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r3.claim: When the star set, Abraham showed its deficiency: a deity should not disappear; he would not take as god something that rises, moves, and passes from place to place.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r3.anchor: أراهم النقص الداخل على النجم بالأفول؛ لأنه ليس [ينبغي] (¬1) [لإله] (¬2) أن يزول ولا أن يغيب

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r4.claim: A second sound interpretation takes Abraham's words as an argument using his people's own assumption: ‘this is my Lord’ means ‘according to you and your claim,’ like God's ironic address to those who imagine partners.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r4.anchor: وقيل: إنه قال: {هذا ربي} على جهة الاحتجاج على قومه لا على معنى الشك

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r5.claim: A third interpretation supplies an unspoken ‘you say’: Abraham asks his people to say that the star is his Lord, as Arabic and Qur'anic speech often omits the verb ‘say.’
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p245/r5.anchor: وجائز أن يكون هاهنا إضمار القول كأنه قال: [تقولون] (¬3): {هذا ربي}

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p247/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p247/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p247/r1.claim: The author classifies three sound interpretations: the first is al-Farrāʾ's and chosen by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim; al-Zajjāj and Ibn al-Anbārī give the second and third.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p247/r1.anchor: فهذه ثلاثة أوجه صحيحة في تأويل الآية، ذكرها أهل المعاني، الوجه الأول: قول الفراء

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p247/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p247/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p247/r2.claim: The statement ‘I do not love those that set’ proves that whatever disappears after appearing is no Lord; alternation between rising and setting shows a created, governed, controlled thing, inconsistent with divinity.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p247/r2.anchor: وفي قوله: {لا أحب الآفلين} دلالة على أن ما غاب بعد ظهوره فليس برب

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:75-78/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:75-78/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:75-78/r5.claim: The night covering Abraham means that it darkened.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:75-78/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:75-78/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:75-78/r6.claim: Abraham's statement that the star was his lord voices what star-governance believers claimed; his people thought stars governed creation.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:75-78/r6.anchor: أي: في زعمكم أيها القائلون بحكم النجم، وذلك أنهم كانوا أصحاب نجوم يرون التدبير في الخليقة لها

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:75-78/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:75-78/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:75-78/r7.claim: By observing that the star set, Abraham exposed their error: something that disappears after appearing is originated and subjugated, not a lord.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:75-78/r7.anchor: عرفهم جهلهم وخطأهم في تعظيم النجوم، ودل على أن من غاب بعد الظهور كان حادثا مسخرا، وليس برب.

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses afalat as moving away from the middle of the sky, with a line by Kaʿb ibn Malik offered as Arabic usage evidence.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r4.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: زالت عن كبد السماء. وضاهده قول كعب بن مالك

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r5.claim: The zenith gloss is approximate; the word also evokes setting and disappearance at sunset.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r5.anchor: وتفسير أفول الشمس بزوالها عن كبد السماء، هو من قبيل الشرح على وجه التقريب، فلا يفوتنا معه لمحُ ما في الأفول من دلالة الغروب

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r6.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r6.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r6.claim: The Qur'an uses aful only of the star, moon, and sun, whose light disappears when they set.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r6.anchor: والقرآن لم يستعمله إلا في النيرات: الكوكب والقمر والشمس، إذ يغيب ضوؤها في مغيب الغروب

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r7.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r7.speaker: أبو عبيدة
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r7.claim: Abu Ubayda explains afala as disappeared.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r7.anchor: وفي مجاز القرآن لأبي عبيدة: {فَلَمَّا أَفَلَ} أي غاب

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r8.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r8.speaker: الهروي
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r8.claim: Al-Harawi explains the phrase as referring to things that disappear and notes that stars are said to set when they disappear.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r8.anchor: وفي الغريبين للهروى: {لَا أُحِبُّ الْآفِلِينَ} أي التي تغيب، يقال أفلتى النجوم إذا غابت

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r9.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r9.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r9.claim: Bint al-Shati suggests the word may derive from al-afil, a wet nurse whose milk has dried up.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p423/r9.anchor: ولعله منقول من الآفل: المرضع ذهب لبنها

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r7.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r7.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r7.claim: The word is read with tafkhīm, imāla, or an intermediate pronunciation, and with either kasra or fatḥa on rāʾ and hamza.
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r7.anchor: يقرا بالإمالة والتفخيم وبين ذلك وبكسر الراء والهمزة وفتحهما

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r8.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r8.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r8.claim: Tafkhīm preserves the original form: yāʾ became alif when the preceding vowel opened, though the written form retains yāʾ to distinguish roots.
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r8.anchor: فالحجة لمن فخم أنه أتى باللفظة على أصل ما وجب لها لأن الياء قد انقلبت بالحركة ألفا وإنما كتبت في السواد ياء للفرق بين ذوات الواو والياء

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r9.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r9.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r9.claim: Imāla begins with the original yāʾ for ease, then spreads to the adjacent hamza; its imāla is due to proximity rather than its own root.
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r9.anchor: والحجة لمن أمال أنه أعمل اللسان من وجه واحد طلبا للتخفيف فأمال الياء في اللفظ ثم نحا بالكسرة إلى الهمزة فأمالها للمجاورة

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r10.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r10.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r10.claim: Bayna-bayna takes a middle course between two dialectal pronunciations.
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r10.anchor: والحجة لمن قرأها بين بين أنه عدل بين اللفظين وأخذ بأوسط اللغتين

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r11.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r11.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r11.claim: Imāla of hamza and the preceding rāʾ follows adjacent letters, as shown by the word-level spread of kasra in a cited parallel.
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r11.anchor: والحجة لمن أمال الهمزة والراء قبلها فإنه أتبع بعض الحروف بعضا بالإمالة

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r12.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r12.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r12.claim: Before alif-lām, the preferred reading is tafkhīm because yāʾ disappears in pronunciation and its imāla no longer applies; one report of rāʾ kasra and hamza fatḥa is called weak.
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p142/r12.anchor: فأما قوله ﴿ رأى القمر ﴾ وما شاكله مما تستقبله ألف ولام فالوجه فيه التفخيم والإمالة مطروحة

QUSHAYRI:v1p299/r12.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p299/r12.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p299/r12.claim: One reading shows Abraham passing from star-like intellect and proof, to moon-like knowledge and evidence, then to sun-like gnosis, where doubt and concealment vanish.
QUSHAYRI:v1p299/r12.anchor: فطلع نجم العقول فشاهد الحق بسره بنور البرهان ، فقال : هذا ربي

QUSHAYRI:v1p299/r14.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p299/r14.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p299/r14.claim: An alternative reading has Abraham first see created signs through God, then see things as belonging to and coming from God, and finally behold them effaced in God.
QUSHAYRI:v1p299/r14.anchor: كان يلاحظ الآثار والأغيار بالله ، ثم كان يرى الأشياء لله ومن الله

IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p203/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p203/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p203/r1.claim: A report says Abraham saw people sinning in the realm of dominion and prayed against them; God told him to stop, since a servant might have good offspring, repent, or face the Fire.
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p203/r1.anchor: فروي: أنه رأى في الملكوت عبدا على فاحشة

IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p203/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p203/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p203/r2.claim: Ibn Qutayba rejects reading Abraham's words as sincere belief that a star was God: after seeing the kingdom to gain certainty he could not then believe the star was his Lord.
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p203/r2.anchor: أفترى الله أراه الملكوت ليوقن، فلما أيقن رأى كوكبا

BURHAN:v3p469/r4.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p469/r4.speaker: author
BURHAN:v3p469/r4.claim: Zarkashī reads the setting celestial body, which he glosses here as the moon, as a second-figure syllogism: it sets, unlike the Lord, so it is not the Lord; setting also proves origination and an originator.
BURHAN:v3p469/r4.anchor: فالقمر ليس بربي أثبته بقياس اقتراني جلى من الشكل الثاني واحتج بالتعبير على الحدوث والحدوث على المحدث

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r1.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r1.claim: The two poems differ in choosing day or night for a visit, but their poetic substance and the specific feature under discussion are alike, not opposites.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r1.anchor: هذه القطعة ضد الأولى من حيث اختار النهار وقتا للزيارة في تلك والليل في هذه فأما من حيث يختلف جوهر الشعر ويتفق

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r2.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r2.claim: The definite ‘moon’ can suggest the actual moon, while plural ‘moons’ suggests a second moon and admits metaphor; ‘I am a sun’ similarly nearly admits a second sun.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r2.anchor: فقوله البدر بالتعريف مع قوله لا أحب تغيير رسمي وتركه أن يقول رسم مثلى يخيل إليك البدر نفسه

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r3.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r3.claim: Al-Mutanabbi’s ‘two moons at once’ means the woman’s face as the sun together with the moon itself; definiteness and simultaneity only make sense if he imagines her as the sun.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r3.anchor: لولا تخيل أنها الشمس نفسها لم يكن لتغليب اسم القمر والتعريف بالألف واللام معنى

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r4.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r4.claim: Abū al-Fatḥ’s comparison captures the general mental image of the verse about the gazelle and sunlight, but not its particular poetic craft.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p273/r4.anchor: فتشبيه على الجملة ومن حيث أصل المعنى وصورته في المعقول فاما الصورة الخاصة التي تحدث له بالصنعة فلم يعرض لها

BURHAN:v2p134/r1.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v2p134/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURHAN:v2p134/r1.claim: Abraham’s rejection of setting stars supports the Prophet’s report that the source of fitna and disbelief is toward the east; repentance’s door opens from the west.
BURHAN:v2p134/r1.anchor: ما يبين تصديق النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في قوله رأس الفتنة والكفر نحو المشرق

BURHAN:v3p212/r3.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p212/r3.speaker: author
BURHAN:v3p212/r3.claim: The interrogative hamza is omitted in Abraham's 'this is my lord'; the intended wording is a question, 'Is this my lord?'

IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p202/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p202/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p202/r1.claim: Abraham’s statement about the star is a staged argument: he feigns the community’s reverence to gain their trust, then shows that a setting star cannot be God and applies the lesson to moon and sun without provocation.
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p202/r1.anchor: يريد: أن يستدرجهم بهذا القول، ويعرفهم خطأهم، وجهلهم في تعظيمهم شأن النجوم

IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p202/r3.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p202/r3.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p202/r3.claim: The author compares Abraham’s strategy to a ḥawārī who feigned devotion to an idol, exposed its inability to help against an enemy, and then led its worshippers to pray to God, who delivered them.
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p202/r3.anchor: ومثل هذا: الحواري حين ورد على قوم يعبدون (بدا) لهم فأظهر تعظيمه

IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p202/r4.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p202/r4.speaker: من الناس
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p202/r4.claim: Some claim Abraham was then in error and confusion; Ibn Qutayba rejects this because God protected and purified him, citing his sound heart and exegetes who say he never associated anything with God.
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p202/r4.anchor: ومن الناس من يذهب إلى أن إبراهيم صلى الله عليه وسلم، كان في تلك الحال على ضلال وحيرة

IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p201/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p201/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p201/r1.claim: Ibn Qutayba places Abraham in an age of astrology and divination, when people revered stars and claimed they foretold hidden events; Nimrod ordered newborns killed after astrologers predicted Abraham’s birth.
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p201/r1.anchor: عصر نجوم وكهانة، وإنما أمر نمروذ

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r3.claim: Kawkab means a star, is used in several senses, and can denote something shining with fire.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r3.anchor: والكوكبة النجم وهو مشترك بين معان كثيرة ويقال كوكب توقد

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r4.speaker: الصاغاني
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r4.claim: Al-Saghani says the word kawkab should be listed under the root واو كاف باء because its initial kaf is augmentative.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r4.anchor: وقال الصاغاني: حق لفظ كوكب أن يذكر في تركيب وك ب عند حذاق النحويين فإنها صدرت بكاف زائدة

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r5.speaker: الجوهري والليث
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r5.claim: Al-Jawhari lists the word as كوكب, perhaps following al-Layth, who regarded the waw as original and the word as quadriliteral.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r5.anchor: إلا أن الجوهري أوردها في تركيب ك وك ب ولعله تبع فيه الليث فإنه ذكره في الرباعي ذاهبا إلى أن الواو أصلية

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r6.claim: Abu Hayyan questions which exacting grammarians accept an augmentative kaf, especially as the first letter of a word.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r6.anchor: وليت شعري من حذاق النحويين الذين تكون الكاف عندهم من حروف الزيادة فضلا عن زيادتها في أول كلمة

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r7.claim: He argues that Hindaki is not evidence for an added kaf: the alleged Arab form is like the paired forms sabt and sabtar, and the poet's henadek means people of India.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r7.anchor: هندي وهندكي في معنى واحد وهو المنسوب إلى الهند قال الشاعر

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r8.claim: Abu Hayyan explains Hindaki as an Ethiopian nisba pattern transmitted through contact; Ethiopians add a softened kasra-kaf and ya, sometimes replacing it with ta, and the languages share vocabulary and grammatical patterns.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r8.anchor: والحبشة إذا نسبت ألحقت آخر ما تنسب إليه كافا مكسورة مشوبة بعدها ياء

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r9.claim: Jan al-layl and ajanna mean that night darkened or covered something; the form is transitive in the sense of covering.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r9.anchor: جن عليه الليل وأجن أظلم هذا تفسير المعنى وهو بمعنى ستر متعديا

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r10.claim: An anonymous poetic citation uses janna in the sense of covering, in the line about water visited before sleep and covered by dark twilight.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r10.anchor: وماء وردت قبيل الكرى ... وقد جنه السدف الأدهم

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v4p557#3/r11.claim: Afala, yafilu, afulan means to disappear or set.
